Although appropriate specialist information is available (verified_patient_facts: blackout.appropriate_specialist_information_available = true), the guidelines state that for undetermined mechanisms, fitness must be assessed according to section 1.3 regarding medical standards not covered in the specific blackout standards. The current data does not confirm whether the condition can be diagnosed as syncope, seizure, or another treatable condition, nor does it confirm the absence of recurrence risk sufficient for an unconditional licence under commercial rules. 1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-BLK-COM-004
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
Where a person with one or more blackouts 
of undetermined mechanism does not 
meet the standards above for a conditional 
licence but may, in the opinion of the 
treating specialist, be safe to drive, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority, subject to at 
least annual review:
•	 if the driver licensing authority, after 
considering information provided by the 
treating specialist(s), considers that the 
risk of a crash caused by a blackout is 
acceptably low.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

4. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

4. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

Where a person with one or more blackouts

conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority, subject to at 
least annual review:

considering information provided by the 
treating specialist(s), considers that the 
risk of a crash caused by a blackout is 
acceptably low.

vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
Where a person with one or more blackouts 
of undetermined mechanism does not 
meet the standards above for a conditional 
licence but may, in the opinion of the 
treating specialist, be safe to drive, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority, subject to at 
least annual review:
•	 if the driver licensing authority, after 
considering information provided by the 
treating specialist(s), considers that the 
risk of a crash caused by a blackout is 
acceptably low.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

4. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

{
  "assessment_outcome": "insufficient_information",
  "explanation": "The patient has experienced two blackouts of undetermined mechanism separated by at least 24 hours. According to guideline evidence (AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d55576d02, AFTD2022-BLK-COM-004, AFTD2022-BLK-COM-005), a person should not drive for 10 years following two or more such blackouts. The verified facts confirm blackout.years_since_last_event = 10 and blackout.episodes_separated_by_24h_count = 2. However, the guidelines state that a conditional licence may be considered only if there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years AND information provided by an appropriate specialist confirms the criterion is met. While appropriate_specialist_information_available is true, the specific clinical criterion regarding the absence of recurrence over the full 10-year period cannot be definitively established as 'met' solely based on the time elapsed without explicit confirmation from the specialist that the risk has been sufficiently mitigated for commercial driving. Furthermore, the mechanism remains undetermined (blackout.diagnosis = 'undetermined'), which precludes a standard unconditional licence and requires strict adherence to conditional criteria that are not fully satisfied by the available data points alone. Therefore, an assessment outcome cannot be established as fit or unfit without further explicit confirmation of the specialist's judgment on the specific criterion.",
  "source_ids": [
    "AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02",
    "AFTD2022-BLK-COM-004",

  ],

  ]
}
1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

5. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

5. AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee
Section 1.3 · PDF 71 · Printed page 60 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
Where a person with one or more blackouts 
of undetermined mechanism does not 
meet the standards above for a conditional 
licence but may, in the opinion of the 
treating specialist, be safe to drive, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority, subject to at 
least annual review:
•	 if the driver licensing authority, after 
considering information provided by the 
treating specialist(s), considers that the 
risk of a crash caused by a blackout is 
acceptably low.

A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

approach should be considered for commercial

4. AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.1. General considerations1–4
Blackouts may occur due to a range of 
mechanisms including:
•	
vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts 
for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and 
may be due to factors such as hot weather, 
emotion or venepuncture but may also be 
due to more serious causes that may recur
•	
syncope due to other cardiovascular causes 
such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias 
or vascular disease
•	
epileptic seizure, which accounts for less 
than 10 per cent of blackouts
•	
other causes including metabolic causes 
(e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a 
sleep disorder.
Determination of the mechanism of a blackout 
may be straightforward based on history, 
investigations and specialist referral, and the 
person may be managed as per the appropriate 
chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
5. AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
cardiovascular and neurological investigations 
and referral to several specialists. People should 
be advised not to drive until the mechanism is 
ascertained and the corresponding standard met.
Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving 
mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event 
that occurred for some other reason such as 
inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone 
conversation). There will also be a small 
proportion of cases in which a clear cause 
cannot be established.

mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

themselves with the information in this chapter 
and the tabulated standards before assessing a

be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure

4. AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.1. General considerations1–4
Blackouts may occur due to a range of 
mechanisms including:
•	
vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts 
for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and 
may be due to factors such as hot weather, 
emotion or venepuncture but may also be 
due to more serious causes that may recur
•	
syncope due to other cardiovascular causes 
such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias 
or vascular disease
•	
epileptic seizure, which accounts for less 
than 10 per cent of blackouts
•	
other causes including metabolic causes 
(e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a 
sleep disorder.
Determination of the mechanism of a blackout 
may be straightforward based on history, 
investigations and specialist referral, and the 
person may be managed as per the appropriate 
chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
5. AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
cardiovascular and neurological investigations 
and referral to several specialists. People should 
be advised not to drive until the mechanism is 
ascertained and the corresponding standard met.
Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving 
mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event 
that occurred for some other reason such as 
inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone 
conversation). There will also be a small 
proportion of cases in which a clear cause 
cannot be established.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

Consequently, first principles must be applied regarding the likelihood of recurrence and treatability. While hypoglycaemia is generally treatable, the established fact that a blackout has occurred creates an unresolved risk for commercial driving without further management data (e.g., current glycemic control, absence of symptoms during driving). The guideline explicitly states people should not drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met; since no specific standard covers this diagnosis and recurrence cannot be ruled out based on the provided facts, fitness cannot be established. 1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.
3. AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006
Section 1.3 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
themselves with the information in this chapter 
and the tabulated standards before assessing a 
person’s fitness to drive.

standard appropriate to the condition should 
be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 
6. Management of blackouts and driving). For 
blackouts due to medical causes not covered 
in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – 
general guidance). For blackouts where, after

4. AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.1. General considerations1–4
Blackouts may occur due to a range of 
mechanisms including:
•	
vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts 
for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and 
may be due to factors such as hot weather, 
emotion or venepuncture but may also be 
due to more serious causes that may recur
•	
syncope due to other cardiovascular causes 
such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias 
or vascular disease
•	
epileptic seizure, which accounts for less 
than 10 per cent of blackouts
•	
other causes including metabolic causes 
(e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a 
sleep disorder.
Determination of the mechanism of a blackout 
may be straightforward based on history, 
investigations and specialist referral, and the 
person may be managed as per the appropriate 
chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
5. AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
cardiovascular and neurological investigations 
and referral to several specialists. People should 
be advised not to drive until the mechanism is 
ascertained and the corresponding standard met.
Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving 
mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event 
that occurred for some other reason such as 
inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone 
conversation). There will also be a small 
proportion of cases in which a clear cause 
cannot be established.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.
3. AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006

themselves with the information in this chapter 
and the tabulated standards before assessing a

4. AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.1. General considerations1–4
Blackouts may occur due to a range of 
mechanisms including:
•	
vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts 
for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and 
may be due to factors such as hot weather, 
emotion or venepuncture but may also be 
due to more serious causes that may recur
•	
syncope due to other cardiovascular causes 
such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias 
or vascular disease
•	
epileptic seizure, which accounts for less 
than 10 per cent of blackouts
•	
other causes including metabolic causes 
(e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a 
sleep disorder.
Determination of the mechanism of a blackout 
may be straightforward based on history, 
investigations and specialist referral, and the 
person may be managed as per the appropriate 
chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
5. AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973
Section 1.2.1 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
cardiovascular and neurological investigations 
and referral to several specialists. People should 
be advised not to drive until the mechanism is 
ascertained and the corresponding standard met.
Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving 
mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event 
that occurred for some other reason such as 
inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone 
conversation). There will also be a small 
proportion of cases in which a clear cause 
cannot be established.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.
2. AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006

and the tabulated standards before assessing a 
person’s fitness to drive.

be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 
6. Management of blackouts and driving). For 
blackouts due to medical causes not covered 
in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – 
general guidance). For blackouts where, after 
investigation, it is not possible to diagnose one 
of the conditions covered elsewhere in this 
publication, refer to the table for blackouts of 
uncertain nature over the page.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0
Section 1.2.4 · PDF 69 · Printed page 58 · Original PDF
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined 
mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.

acceptably low.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01
Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.
2. AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006

themselves with the information in this chapter 
and the tabulated standards before assessing a

be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure

in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to

mechanism
If, despite extensive investigation, the 
mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, 
fitness to drive should be assessed according 
to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. 
The standards for blackout of undetermined 
mechanism are similar to those for seizure.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

Section 1.2.3 · PDF 68 · Printed page 57 · Original PDF
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical 
causes not covered in the standards
If the cause of the blackout is determined 
to be a medical condition not covered in 
the standards, then first principles regarding 
fitness to drive should be applied (refer to 
Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive 
– general guidance). Considerations include 
the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and 
the treatability of the condition as well as the 
nature of the driving task. There should also be 
an appropriate review period. A more stringent 
approach should be considered for commercial 
vehicle drivers.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02
Section 1.3 · PDF 70 · Printed page 59 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods 
driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person should not drive for 5 
years following a single blackout of 
undetermined nature.
A person should not drive for 10 years 
following two or more blackouts of 
undetermined nature separated by a 24-
hour period.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has experienced blackouts 
that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, 
seizure or another condition.
If there has been a single blackout or more 
than one blackout within a 24-hour period, 
a conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to 
at least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 5 years.
If there have been two or more blackouts 
separated by at least 24 hours, a 
conditional licence may be considered by 
the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into account 
information provided by an appropriate 
specialist as to whether the following 
criterion is met:
•	 there have been no further blackouts for 
at least 10 years.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

{
  "assessment_outcome": "meets_unconditional_standard",
  "explanation": "The patient has diabetes treated by diet and exercise only, which does not disqualify them from holding an unconditional commercial driver's licence. 1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
2. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008

•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

While the nurse note mentions specialist information is available, this is a prerequisite for conditional assessments; since the non-insulin treatment category allows for unrestricted driving provided the clinical criteria are met, the availability of specialist notes does not alter the outcome from 'conditional' to 'unconditional'. Other modules (cardiovascular, vision, hearing) do not impose restrictions based on the provided verified facts.",

1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
2. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

According to guideline AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27, a person is not fit for an unconditional licence if they have non-insulin treated diabetes and are being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. However, the same source states that such a person may drive without restriction if specific criteria are met: no recent history of severe hypoglycaemic events, presence of early warning symptoms (awareness), adherence to a regimen minimizing hypoglycaemia risk, and absence of driving-relevant end-organ effects. The verified facts confirm the patient has diabetes present but not gestational, is acutely well and metabolically stable, has no recent or current severe hypoglycaemic events, possesses hypoglycaemia awareness, follows a regimen that minimises hypoglycaemia, and has no driving-relevant end-organ effects.
