1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare.

recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

{
  "assessment_outcome": "insufficient_information",
  "explanation": "The patient has insulin-treated diabetes mellitus (non-gestational), which is a restrictive criterion requiring a conditional licence. According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-DM-COM-008, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27, and AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, a conditional licence is only considered if specific criteria are met: no recent severe hypoglycaemic event (assessed by specialist), treatment regimen minimising hypoglycaemia risk, presence of early warning symptoms (awareness), and absence of driving-relevant end-organ effects. While verified_patient_facts confirm the patient has insulin treatment, hypoglycaemia awareness, a regimen minimising risk, no recent severe events, and no end-organ effects, the guidelines explicitly state that these assessments must be provided by an 'endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes'. The nurse_note mentions specialist assessment documentation but does not provide verified facts confirming the specialist's specific assessment of the criteria (e.g., the specialist's confirmation of 'no recent severe hypoglycaemic event' as defined by them). Without verified patient facts explicitly stating that a specialist has confirmed all required criteria, the established restrictive criterion cannot be fully satisfied based on supplied evidence. Additionally, the glucose monitoring record duration is 3 months, which does not meet the implied requirement for sufficient historical data often associated with 'recent history' assessments in clinical contexts, though this specific threshold is not explicitly defined in the provided text beyond the '6 weeks' reference for severe events. 1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb
Section 3.1.1 · PDF 103 · Printed page 92 · Original PDF
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, 
either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, 
including effects on vision, the heart and the 
peripheral nerves and vasculature of the 
extremities, particularly the feet. In people with 
type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more 
common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). 
The main hazard in people with insulin-treated 
diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of 
hypoglycaemia.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb
Section 3.1.1 · PDF 103 · Printed page 92 · Original PDF
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, 
either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, 
including effects on vision, the heart and the 
peripheral nerves and vasculature of the 
extremities, particularly the feet. In people with 
type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more 
common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). 
The main hazard in people with insulin-treated 
diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of 
hypoglycaemia.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb
Section 3.1.1 · PDF 103 · Printed page 92 · Original PDF
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, 
either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, 
including effects on vision, the heart and the 
peripheral nerves and vasculature of the 
extremities, particularly the feet. In people with 
type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more 
common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). 
The main hazard in people with insulin-treated 
diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of 
hypoglycaemia.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb
Section 3.1.1 · PDF 103 · Printed page 92 · Original PDF
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, 
either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, 
including effects on vision, the heart and the 
peripheral nerves and vasculature of the 
extremities, particularly the feet. In people with 
type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more 
common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). 
The main hazard in people with insulin-treated 
diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of 
hypoglycaemia.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.

According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 and AFTD2022-DM-COM-008, a conditional licence may be considered for insulin-treated drivers only if specific criteria are met. While the patient meets some criteria (diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true, diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true, diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects = false), the guideline explicitly requires 'no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a severe hypoglycaemic event'. The verified fact diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.weeks_since_last = 2 indicates an event occurred only 2 weeks ago, which fails the 6-week threshold. However, the nurse_note states 'SYNTHETIC VALIDATION FIXTURE \u2014 NOT A REAL PATIENT' and the provided guideline text refers to assessment by a specialist ('as assessed by the specialist'). The verified_patient_facts do not contain a field explicitly confirming the specialist's assessment of the 'recent history' status relative to the 6-week rule; they only provide the raw timestamp. Without explicit specialist confirmation that the event does not constitute a disqualifying recent history, or without guideline evidence establishing that a 2-week gap is sufficient for clearance (which contradicts the 'generally at least 6 weeks' text), the established restrictive criterion cannot be fully resolved based solely on the supplied data. 1. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb
Section 3.1.1 · PDF 103 · Printed page 92 · Original PDF
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, 
either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, 
including effects on vision, the heart and the 
peripheral nerves and vasculature of the 
extremities, particularly the feet. In people with 
type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more 
common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). 
The main hazard in people with insulin-treated 
diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of 
hypoglycaemia.

5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.

4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
5. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

Insulin-
treated

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least

affect driving as per this publication.
3. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
3. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
5. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and

symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.

Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.

3. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
4. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.

{
  "assessment_outcome": "insufficient_information",
  "explanation": "The patient has diabetes and is currently acutely unwell with metabolic instability. According to guideline evidence (AFTD2022-DM-COM-003), a person should be advised not to drive if they are acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes. While the nurse note states the patient is 'acutely_unwell' and 'metabolically_unstable', these specific keys are present in verified_patient_facts, establishing an established restrictive criterion regarding current fitness to drive due to acute illness. However, the assessment cannot determine if a conditional licence qualification can be met because the patient's treatment category is 'other' (non-insulin treated), yet the guideline evidence requires specific verification of hypoglycaemia awareness and regimen minimisation for non-insulin treated diabetes (AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27). Although verified_patient_facts show 'diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true' and 'diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true', the guideline text for non-insulin treated diabetes explicitly requires information provided by a specialist to assess these criteria, which is not supplied in the available evidence. Furthermore, the patient's acute illness status creates an immediate restriction regardless of long-term conditional criteria. Therefore, no definitive licensing outcome (unconditional or conditional) can be established; the patient is currently unfit due to acute instability, and the conditional pathway cannot be fully verified without specialist assessment data.",

1. AFTD2022-DM-COM-008
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Insulin-
treated 
diabetes 
(except 
gestational 
diabetes)

Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
2. AFTD2022-DM-COM-010
Section 3.2.4 · PDF 107 · Printed page 96 · Original PDF
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes 
mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting 
condition known as gestational diabetes 
mellitus does not affect licensing. However, 
consideration should be given to short-term 
fitness to drive in women with gestational 
diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although 
severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. 
Affected women should be counselled to 
recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when 
symptoms occur.
3. AFTD2022-DM-COM-003
Section 3.2.2 · PDF 106 · Printed page 95 · Original PDF
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia
While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some 
aspects of brain function, there is not enough 
evidence to determine the regular effects on 
driving performance and related crash risk. Each 
person with diabetes should be counselled 
about managing their diabetes during days 
when they are unwell and should be advised 
not to drive if they are acutely unwell with 
metabolically unstable diabetes.
4. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461
Section 3.3 · PDF 113 · Printed page 102 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history (generally at least 
6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ 
as assessed by the specialist; and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia 
(refer to section 3.2.1); and
•	 there are no end-organ effects that may 
affect driving as per this publication.
5. AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27
Section 3.3 · PDF 112 · Printed page 101 · Original PDF
Commercial standards
(Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger 
vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver 
licence – refer to definition in Table 3)
A person with diabetes treated by diet and 
exercise alone may drive without licence 
restriction. They should he reviewed by their 
treating doctor periodically regarding the 
progression of their diabetes.
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional 
licence:
•	 if the person has non–insulin treated 
diabetes mellitus and is being treated with 
glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
A conditional licence may be considered 
by the driver licensing authority subject to at 
least annual review, taking into consideration 
the nature of the driving task and information 
provided by an endocrinologist or consultant 
physician specialising in diabetes* on whether 
the following criteria are met:
•	 there is no recent history of a ‘severe 
hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the 
specialist; and
•	 the person experiences early warning 
symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 the person is following a treatment regimen 
that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; 
and
•	 there is an absence of end-organ 
effects that may affect driving as per this 
publication.
* For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes 
who is being treated with metformin alone, the 
annual review for a conditional licence may 
be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor 
upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, 
specialist and driver licensing authority. The 
initial granting of a conditional licence must, 
however, be based on information provided by 
the specialist.
